clue.text: Tests were designed to keep one cool

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within, so the rearranged letters go around the next piece
tests that were designed have been put together in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Some examinations were set up to make sure a person stays calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'designed' rearranges TESTS WERE, and 'to keep' puts I (one) inside the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Streetwise means savvy about urban life, and in slang being cool implies that same knowing, unflappable style.

clue.text: Father ultimately shows anger

indicators.note: take what comes at the very end of the next word

parts.note: the final letter of SHOWS
ire = anger

explanation.surface: A dad finally losing his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: "Ultimately" looks like it belongs with Father, as in the end he snaps, but it acts on "shows".
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used mostly of animals: a stallion that sires foals is their father, and breeders list the sire and the dam.

clue.text: Dream I will be held in respect

indicators.note: one piece is held inside another

parts.note: to revere is to respect deeply
I stays as it is, placed inside REVER…E

explanation.surface: Someone hoping that one day they will be admired.
explanation.walkthrough: "I will be held in respect" reads as an ambition; the "I" is simply the letter going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the waking sense: a reverie is a daydream, a spell of being lost in pleasant thoughts.

clue.text: NHS timetables ruined business

indicators.note: a ruined schedule is wrecked and jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that Health Service schedules have wrecked trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' signals that the letters of NHS TIMETABLES are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An establishment is a commercial firm or institution, a sense shared with business as a noun for a company.

clue.text: Climber regularly waits at sea, wind rising

indicators.note: regularly means taking letters at even intervals, here the first, third, fifth and so on

parts.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of these words

indicators.note: in a down clue, something rising is read from bottom to top, so the word is turned backwards

parts.note: air is a gentle wind or breeze

explanation.surface: Someone loiters at sea while the breeze picks up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes alternate letters of WAITS AT SEA, giving WISTE; 'rising' turns AIR (wind) upwards into RIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisteria is a vine that twines up walls and trellises, so it is a plant described as a climber.

clue.text: Vocally scares away e.g. animals or trainers?

definitions.note: Covers the verb (a farrier shoes horses) and the noun (trainers are shoes).

indicators.note: the next part is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: to shoo is to scare away

explanation.surface: Someone shouting to drive off animals or sports coaches.
explanation.walkthrough: "Trainers" looks like people who train animals, which fits the surface; it is the British word for sports shoes. Shoeing animals is what a blacksmith does to horses.
explanation.definitionFit: One shoes animals such as horses, and trainers are a kind of shoes.

clue.text: Fools around in places for pampering

indicators.note: the word is turned around

parts.note: saps = fools, gullible people; this word is the one turned around

explanation.surface: Idiots messing about at a health resort.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fools around" reads as a single verb phrase, messing about; split it into noun and turning instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Spas are resorts where people go to be pampered.

clue.text: Quietly put down writing instrument — small child here?

parts.note: p = piano, quietly in music
to lay is to put down
a pen writes

explanation.surface: Softly setting down a pen, with a toddler nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a hint rather than a synonym, flagged by the question mark: a playpen is where a small child is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A playpen is an enclosure where a small child is put to play safely.

clue.text: Laugh about a young man dressing

indicators.note: the laugh word goes about the other letters

parts.note: a scream is something hilarious, a laugh
a lad is a young man

explanation.surface: It's a laugh to see a young man getting dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' looks like putting clothes on; it is a sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: Salad cream is a creamy yellow condiment, a British salad dressing.

clue.text: Fix components of motor I've tested

indicators.note: the answer is made of parts of the following words

parts.note: motoR I'VE Tested

explanation.surface: A mechanic reporting on engine parts they have checked.
explanation.walkthrough: The mechanical surface makes "components" look like engine parts, which hides the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To rivet is to fix something firmly, as with metal pins.

clue.text: Deficit the result of brief American season

parts.note: brief = short
Americans call autumn fall

explanation.surface: A financial gap blamed on a short American autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: "American" is there because only in American English is the season called fall; British English says autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortfall is a deficit, an amount by which something falls short.

clue.text: Dish, one hotel had it prepared

indicators.note: food that is prepared has been made up, so the letters are made up again in a new order

explanation.surface: A hotel made one meal for a guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared' rearranges the letters of ONE HOTEL HAD IT. Toad-in-the-hole is a British dish of sausages baked in Yorkshire pudding batter.
explanation.definitionFit: Toad-in-the-hole is a traditional British meal of sausages in batter, so it is an example of a dish.

clue.text: Smooth unusually bad tempers having been automatically approved

parts.note: to rub something is to smooth it by friction

indicators.note: unusually means arranged in an odd way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone with oddly bad moods was given the nod without scrutiny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth' looks like an adjective for the approval, but it is a verb giving the first three letters; 'unusually' shuffles the bad tempers.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubber-stamped describes a decision passed routinely without real scrutiny, which is approval given mechanically.

clue.text: Man getting the sack, the present supremo?

definitions.meaning: the surface reading is a man being fired; the meant reading is a man handed a big bag to carry
the surface reading is the current boss; the meant reading is the one in charge of gifts

explanation.surface: The current boss being fired.
explanation.walkthrough: "Getting the sack" means being fired, and "present" means current, so the clue reads as office politics; the sack is his bag of gifts and the presents are Christmas ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: both halves describe the Christmas gift-bringer once "sack" and "present" take their literal senses.

clue.text: Drunk pirate providing drink

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so the letters of pirate are jumbled

parts.note: providing means on condition that, which is if

explanation.surface: A tipsy buccaneer is the one supplying the booze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' rearranges PIRATE into APERIT, followed by IF (providing).
explanation.definitionFit: An aperitif is an alcoholic drink taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite.

clue.text: Engage troops for fellow from Rome?

parts.note: to sign someone is to engage them, as a club signs a player
OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Hiring soldiers on behalf of a Roman man.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the definition by example: any Italian man, not only a Roman, is a signor.
explanation.definitionFit: Signor is the Italian for Mr, a title for a man.

clue.text: Empty, set off — pigs in these?

parts.note: blank means empty, as of a page

indicators.note: off here means out of order or wrong, so the letters of set are rearranged

explanation.surface: An empty pen, and the animals have run away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' signals a jumble of SET. Pigs in blankets are a British Christmas dish of small sausages wrapped in bacon, which is the joke behind the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The dish called pigs in blankets is sausages wrapped in bacon, so the bacon covers are what the pigs sit in.

clue.text: Note circulating that hurt? You got me!

indicators.note: the note goes round the next piece

parts.note: te is a note of the sol-fa scale
what you say when something hurts; it sits inside T…E

explanation.surface: Someone conceding a painful point in an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: "That hurt?" is the exclamation OUCH, not a question about pain.
explanation.definitionFit: Touché, from fencing, concedes that an opponent has scored a fair point.

clue.text: Country with bad weather: finally, locate another

parts.note: the United Kingdom
rain = bad weather

indicators.note: take the last letter of the next word

parts.note: the last letter of LOCATE

explanation.surface: Someone fleeing a rainy country to find another one.
explanation.walkthrough: "Country" looks like the definition, but it gives UK; the definition is "another", meaning another country.
explanation.definitionFit: Ukraine is another country, following on from the UK in the wordplay.

clue.text: "Heap" and "lot" possibly about right — for this?

definitions.text: "Heap" and "lot" possibly about right — for this?

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters go around the next piece
possibly signals that the letters can be arranged in another way

explanation.surface: Asks whether heap and lot would be fair words for the thing described.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted words are not the definition alone: they are the anagram fodder, and the whole clue doubles as a description, since heap and lot are fair synonyms for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plethora is an excess or abundance, and heap and lot both mean a large amount.

clue.text: Busy, about to get £200 in Monopoly?

definitions.meaning: busy = constantly active, never sitting still
landing on the starting square in Monopoly collects £200

explanation.surface: A board-game player hurrying round to collect their money.
explanation.walkthrough: In Monopoly, passing or landing on the GO square pays £200, so a piece sitting on the GO square is collecting it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the go is busy and constantly active.

clue.text: Journalist's second report redrafted to include leader of Norway

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so the rearranged letters go around the next piece
a redrafted text is written out again, so the letters of second report are rearranged
the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Norway

explanation.surface: A reporter's follow-up story is rewritten to add the head of a Scandinavian state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'redrafted' rearranges SECOND REPORT, and 'to include' puts N, the 'leader of' Norway, inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A correspondent is a journalist who reports on a particular subject or from a particular place.

clue.text: Great Russian ruler, favourite with our old Queen

parts.note: a teacher's pet is a favourite
ER = Elizabeth Regina, Elizabeth II

explanation.surface: Comparing a tsar with a favourite British monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: "Great" looks like praise, but it is part of the name: Peter the Great.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by epithet: the tsar Peter I, who built St Petersburg, is remembered with "the Great" after his name.

clue.text: Girl showing style, not the first

indicators.note: not the first tells us to drop the opening letter of the word

parts.note: class means style or elegance

explanation.surface: A young woman showing flair, though not the top one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not the first' removes C, the first letter of CLASS (style).
explanation.definitionFit: Lass is a Scottish and northern English word for a young woman, a synonym of girl.

clue.text: Come into view carrying child last of all, he thought

indicators.note: the arising word carries the others inside it

parts.note: to arise is to appear, come into view
a tot is a small child

indicators.note: only the final letter of all is used

parts.note: its last letter is L

explanation.surface: A figure appears holding a child, the last of all, lost in thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He thought' is a playful definition: a thinker, the Greek philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle was the ancient Greek philosopher, famous above all as a thinker.

clue.text: Love large character

parts.note: love = nil = O in tennis
mega = huge

explanation.surface: A fondness for a big personality.
explanation.walkthrough: "Character" reads as a personality; it is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is a character, the last letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Appear with spy and his boss?

parts.note: to spy is to see
M is James Bond's boss, and Bond is a spy

explanation.surface: Turning up with a secret agent and his chief.
explanation.walkthrough: "Spy" works twice: as a verb it gives SEE, and as a noun it sets up "his boss", M in the Bond films.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of giving an impression, not of turning up: "she appears happy".

clue.text: Rich American going after Miranda's father

indicators.note: this piece comes after the next one

parts.note: in Shakespeare's The Tempest, Miranda is the daughter of the exiled duke
US = American

explanation.surface: A wealthy American chasing a woman's father.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rich" could be a man's name to go with Miranda, but it is the definition; the father is the magician of The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: wealthy and flourishing, as a prosperous merchant is.
